items.title: The drug development pipeline
items.explainer: Bringing a new medicine from idea to pharmacy shelf typically takes 10 to 15 years. The pipeline begins with discovery: identifying a biological target linked to a disease and finding molecules that act on it. Promising candidates then enter preclinical testing in cells and animals to assess how they work, how the body handles them, and whether they are toxic. Only then can a drug be tested in people, under an investigational application to a regulator such as the US Food and Drug Administration. Phase I trials give the drug to a small group, often healthy volunteers, mainly to assess safety and dosing. Phase II trials, in a few hundred patients, look for signs of effectiveness and refine the dose. Phase III trials, often in thousands of patients, confirm effectiveness against placebo or existing treatment and detect less common side effects. If the evidence holds up, the company applies for approval, and after approval phase IV monitoring continues to watch for rare problems in the wider population. Attrition is severe: only roughly one in ten drugs that enter phase I eventually reaches approval, most often failing for lack of efficacy or for safety problems. Estimates of total cost per approved drug range widely, often into billions of dollars.

question.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a Phase I clinical trial?

options.text: To assess safety and determine a tolerable dose in a small group of people
To prove the drug works better than existing treatments in thousands of patients
To monitor rare side effects after the drug is on the market
To identify the biological target of the disease

question.explanation: Phase I focuses on safety, tolerability and dosing; efficacy is explored in Phase II and confirmed in Phase III.

items.title: Target identification and validation
items.explainer: Most modern drug programs start by choosing a target: usually a protein, such as an enzyme, receptor or ion channel, whose activity drives a disease and that a drug could plausibly change. Target identification draws on many kinds of evidence. Human genetics is among the most persuasive. If people who carry a naturally occurring mutation that disables a gene are protected from a disease, inhibiting that gene's protein with a drug may protect others too. The classic example is PCSK9: people with loss-of-function variants have very low LDL cholesterol and fewer heart attacks, and drugs blocking PCSK9 followed. Other evidence comes from gene expression studies comparing diseased and healthy tissue, from CRISPR screens that switch off genes one at a time in cells, and from animal models. Validation is the harder step: showing convincingly that modulating the target changes the disease, in a way that will translate to patients. Weak validation is a major reason drugs fail in Phase II, where many compounds hit their target exactly as designed but the patients do not improve, because the target was not truly driving the disease. Analyses of past pipelines have found that drug programs whose targets are supported by human genetic evidence are more likely to succeed in development.

question.prompt: Why are people with natural loss-of-function mutations in a gene valuable for target validation?

options.text: Their mutations can be copied directly into a drug
They show what happens to human health when that protein's activity is reduced
They are exempt from clinical trial requirements
They are immune to all side effects

question.explanation: Such people are a natural experiment: if lifelong reduced activity of the protein is protective and safe, a drug that inhibits it is more likely to work.

items.title: High-throughput screening
items.explainer: Once a target is chosen, chemists need a starting molecule that acts on it. High-throughput screening finds such molecules by brute force. Robots test large libraries of compounds, often hundreds of thousands to millions of them, against the target in miniaturized assays run in plates containing hundreds or thousands of tiny wells. Each well holds the target, for example an enzyme with a substrate that produces light or color when the reaction runs, plus one test compound. Wells where the signal changes in the expected way flag potential hits. Most initial hits are false positives. Some compounds interfere with the assay itself, for instance by absorbing light, aggregating into clumps that nonspecifically disrupt proteins, or reacting chemically with anything they touch. Confirmatory testing, counterscreens and dose-response measurements weed these out, leaving a small set of validated hits. Medicinal chemists then pick the most promising chemical series as leads and begin optimizing them for potency, selectivity and drug-like properties. Alternatives to classical screening include fragment-based discovery, which screens very small molecules and grows them into larger ones, DNA-encoded libraries that tag each compound with a DNA barcode so billions can be tested at once, and computational virtual screening of enormous digital libraries.

question.prompt: Why must hits from a high-throughput screen be confirmed with follow-up tests?

options.text: Robots cannot measure signals accurately
Regulators require every library compound to be retested
Many hits are false positives that interfere with the assay rather than acting on the target
Hits always lose activity after one week

question.explanation: Compounds can mimic activity by disrupting the readout, aggregating or reacting nonspecifically. Counterscreens and dose-response tests separate real binders from artifacts.

items.title: Lipinski's rule of five
items.explainer: Most patients prefer to take a pill, so a drug usually needs to be absorbed from the gut into the bloodstream. In 1997 Christopher Lipinski and colleagues at Pfizer analyzed thousands of compounds that had reached clinical trials and identified simple properties shared by most orally absorbed drugs. Their 'rule of five', named because every threshold is a multiple of five, says poor absorption is more likely when a molecule breaks more than one of these limits: a molecular weight above 500 daltons; a calculated logP, a measure of how strongly it prefers fat over water, above 5; more than 5 hydrogen-bond donors, such as OH and NH groups; and more than 10 hydrogen-bond acceptors, such as nitrogen and oxygen atoms. The logic is physical. To cross the gut wall, a molecule must pass through fatty cell membranes, which favors compounds that are not too large, not too polar, and not too greasy to dissolve in the first place. The rule became a widely used filter for screening libraries and guiding chemists. It is a rule of thumb, not a law. Natural products, antibiotics and drugs absorbed by active transporters often violate it, and newer drug classes such as some macrocycles and targeted protein degraders deliberately operate beyond it.

question.prompt: Under Lipinski's rule of five, which property suggests a compound may be poorly absorbed when taken orally?

options.text: Exactly five carbon atoms
A melting point above 5 degrees Celsius
Fewer than 5 hydrogen-bond donors
A molecular weight above 500 daltons

question.explanation: The rule flags molecular weight over 500, logP over 5, more than 5 H-bond donors and more than 10 H-bond acceptors; breaking more than one limit predicts poor absorption.

items.title: Pharmacokinetics and drug half-life
items.explainer: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug, often summarized as ADME: absorption into the bloodstream, distribution into tissues, metabolism, mostly by liver enzymes such as the cytochrome P450 family, and excretion, mainly through the kidneys. These processes determine how much drug reaches its target and for how long. A central summary number is the elimination half-life, the time for the drug's concentration in the blood to fall by half. It depends on two underlying quantities. Clearance is the volume of blood effectively cleared of the drug per unit of time. Volume of distribution describes how widely the drug spreads into tissues rather than staying in the blood. A larger volume or a lower clearance means a longer half-life. Half-life has direct practical consequences. With repeated dosing, a drug takes about four to five half-lives to approach a steady concentration, and about the same time to wash out after the last dose. A drug with a half-life of a few hours may need dosing several times a day, while one with a half-life of a day or more can be taken once daily. Interactions often work through metabolism: a second drug that blocks a P450 enzyme can raise the first drug's levels to toxic concentrations.

question.prompt: With regular repeated dosing, roughly how long does a drug take to approach steady-state concentration?

options.text: About four to five elimination half-lives
Exactly one half-life
Immediately after the first dose
It never reaches a steady state

question.explanation: Each half-life closes half the remaining gap to steady state, so after four to five half-lives the concentration is within about 94 to 97 percent of its plateau.

items.title: Structure-activity relationships and lead optimization
items.explainer: A screening hit is rarely a drug. It may bind its target weakly, hit other proteins too, be quickly broken down by the liver, or be toxic. Lead optimization is the iterative process in which medicinal chemists make many variants of a promising molecule to fix these problems while keeping its activity. The guiding tool is the structure-activity relationship, or SAR: a systematic map of how changes to a molecule's structure change its biological activity. Chemists might add a methyl group here, swap a hydrogen for a fluorine there, or replace a ring, then measure potency, selectivity and other properties for each variant. Patterns emerge, revealing which parts of the molecule are essential for binding, which can be modified freely, and which cause problems. The objectives frequently conflict. Adding greasy groups may increase potency but reduce solubility and increase metabolic breakdown; blocking a site of metabolism can introduce new toxicity. Optimization is therefore a multi-parameter balancing act, tracked with design-make-test-analyze cycles that may run for years and involve thousands of compounds. Structure-based design, using three-dimensional structures of the target with the molecule bound, and computational models increasingly guide which compounds are worth making, reducing the number of costly syntheses.

question.prompt: What does a structure-activity relationship (SAR) study map out?

options.text: The order in which clinical trial phases are run
How changes in a molecule's structure affect its biological activity
The price of raw chemical materials
How a drug is packaged for sale

question.explanation: SAR links specific structural modifications to changes in potency, selectivity and other properties, guiding which analogs to make next.

items.title: AlphaFold and protein structure prediction
items.explainer: A protein's function depends on the three-dimensional shape its chain of amino acids folds into, and knowing that shape is a powerful aid to drug design. For decades, structures had to be determined experimentally with X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance or cryo-electron microscopy, methods that can take months or years per protein. Predicting structure directly from the amino-acid sequence was a grand challenge of biology. In 2020, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 achieved accuracy comparable to experimental methods for many proteins at the biennial CASP structure-prediction competition. It uses deep learning trained on known structures and on evolutionary information from related protein sequences. Predicted structures for most known proteins were then released in a public database. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work with David Baker, honored for computational protein design. For drug discovery, predicted structures help identify pockets where small molecules might bind and support structure-based design for targets that have never been crystallized. Limits remain. Predictions are less reliable for flexible regions, for the precise positions of side chains in binding sites, and for how a protein changes shape when a drug binds, so experimental validation is still essential before investing heavily in a target.

question.prompt: What problem did AlphaFold 2 largely solve for many proteins in 2020?

options.text: Synthesizing proteins without cells
Running clinical trials without patients
Predicting a protein's 3D structure from its amino-acid sequence
Sequencing the human genome

question.explanation: AlphaFold 2 predicted folded protein structures from sequence with accuracy rivaling experimental methods for many proteins at CASP14.

items.title: Small molecules versus biologics
items.explainer: Medicines fall into two broad families. Small-molecule drugs, such as aspirin, statins and most traditional pills, are chemically synthesized compounds, typically with molecular weights below about 900 daltons. Their small size lets many of them be absorbed from the gut and slip inside cells to reach intracellular targets, and they can be manufactured reproducibly at low cost. Biologics are large molecules made by living cells, such as monoclonal antibodies, therapeutic proteins like insulin, and vaccines. An antibody weighs roughly 150,000 daltons, more than a hundred times a typical small molecule. Biologics can bind large, flat surfaces on proteins that small molecules struggle to grip, and they often achieve exceptional selectivity. But they are usually digested in the stomach, so most must be injected or infused, and they generally cannot enter cells. Manufacturing is complex, since tiny changes in cell culture conditions can alter the product. That complexity shapes competition after patents expire. A generic small molecule can be shown to be chemically identical to the original, while a follow-on biologic, called a biosimilar, must be shown to be highly similar with no clinically meaningful differences, a costlier process. Newer modalities blur the line, including peptides, oligonucleotides, gene therapies and antibody-drug conjugates.

question.prompt: Why must most biologic drugs, such as monoclonal antibodies, be injected rather than taken as pills?

options.text: They are too small to be retained in the body
Regulations forbid oral biologics
They only work when injected into muscle
As large proteins they are broken down in the digestive tract and poorly absorbed

question.explanation: Digestive enzymes degrade proteins, and very large molecules cross the gut wall poorly, so injection or infusion is usually required.

items.title: The therapeutic index
items.explainer: Every drug is toxic at some dose, so the useful question is how far apart the effective dose and the harmful dose are. The therapeutic index summarizes that gap. It is classically defined as the dose that is toxic in 50 percent of subjects divided by the dose that is effective in 50 percent; in animal studies, the lethal dose is sometimes used in place of the toxic dose. A large ratio means a wide safety margin, while a ratio close to one means the effective and toxic doses nearly overlap. Many common drugs have wide margins, so modest dosing errors are rarely dangerous. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index demand care. The anticoagulant warfarin, the heart drug digoxin, the mood stabilizer lithium and certain anti-epilepsy drugs all fall in this category. For such drugs, small changes in dose, diet, kidney function or interacting medications can tip a patient from ineffective to toxic, so doctors measure blood levels or clinical markers, such as clotting time for warfarin, and adjust doses individually. Regulators also apply stricter requirements when generic versions of narrow-index drugs are approved. In development, an inadequate safety margin found in preclinical or early clinical studies is a common reason to abandon a compound.

question.prompt: What does a therapeutic index close to 1 indicate about a drug?

options.text: Its effective and toxic doses nearly overlap, so it needs careful monitoring
It is extremely safe at any dose
It works in exactly one patient out of two
It has no measurable effect

question.explanation: TI = TD50 / ED50. A value near 1 means the dose that causes toxicity is close to the dose that works, leaving little safety margin.

items.title: Drug repurposing
items.explainer: Drug repurposing, also called repositioning, finds new uses for drugs that already exist, either approved medicines or compounds that were shelved after failing for their original purpose. Its appeal is efficiency. Because the drug's safety, dosing and manufacturing have already been studied in people, a repurposed drug can often skip early development steps, reducing cost, time and the risk of failure for safety reasons. Some of the best-known successes were accidental. Sildenafil was developed to treat angina, chest pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart; trial participants reported an unexpected side effect, and it was approved for erectile dysfunction as Viagra, and later for pulmonary arterial hypertension. Thalidomide, notorious for causing birth defects, was later approved under strict controls to treat a complication of leprosy and the blood cancer multiple myeloma. Minoxidil, originally a blood-pressure drug, became a treatment for hair loss after patients grew more hair. Repurposing is increasingly systematic, using analyses of electronic health records, genetic data and computational matching of drug effects to disease signatures. It has limits. Commercial incentives can be weak when the drug is already off-patent and cheap, and some highly publicized repurposing hopes have failed in rigorous randomized trials.

question.prompt: What is the main advantage of repurposing an existing drug compared with developing a new one?

options.text: Repurposed drugs never need clinical trials
Its safety and dosing in humans are already known, saving time and cost
Repurposed drugs always have stronger patent protection
Repurposing guarantees the drug will work for the new disease

question.explanation: Existing human safety and pharmacokinetic data let developers skip or shorten early stages, although efficacy for the new use must still be proven.

items.title: Receptors, agonists and antagonists
items.explainer: Many drugs work by binding to receptors, proteins on or inside cells that normally respond to the body's own signaling molecules, such as hormones and neurotransmitters. A drug that binds a receptor and activates it, mimicking the natural signal, is an agonist. Morphine, for example, activates the mu-opioid receptors that the body's endorphins act on, relieving pain. A drug that binds the receptor without activating it, and so blocks the natural signal, is an antagonist. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist: it binds the same receptors more tightly than morphine or fentanyl, pushes them off, and can reverse an overdose within minutes. Beta blockers such as propranolol are antagonists at receptors for adrenaline, slowing the heart. Between the extremes are partial agonists, which activate a receptor only partly even when every receptor is occupied. Buprenorphine, used to treat opioid addiction, is a partial agonist: it relieves cravings while producing a ceiling on breathing suppression that makes it safer than full agonists. Two separate properties describe a drug at its receptor. Affinity is how tightly it binds, and efficacy is how strongly it activates the receptor once bound. An antagonist can have high affinity but zero efficacy. Prolonged exposure to an agonist can lead the cell to reduce its receptors, which contributes to tolerance.

question.prompt: How does naloxone reverse an opioid overdose?

options.text: It activates opioid receptors more strongly than fentanyl
It breaks down opioids in the blood
It is an antagonist that binds opioid receptors tightly, displacing the opioid without activating them
It stimulates the heart directly

question.explanation: Naloxone has high affinity but no efficacy at opioid receptors, so it displaces the opioid and blocks its effect.

items.title: Dose-response curves, EC50 and IC50
items.explainer: A dose-response curve plots the effect of a drug against its concentration. Because effects usually rise steeply over a narrow range and then level off, the concentration axis is normally drawn on a logarithmic scale, which turns the curve into a characteristic S shape. Two features of the curve summarize a drug. Its height, the maximum effect it can produce, reflects efficacy. Its position along the concentration axis reflects potency, usually reported as the EC50, the concentration that produces half of the maximum effect. For inhibitors, the equivalent is the IC50, the concentration that reduces a target's activity by half. A lower EC50 or IC50 means a more potent drug: less of it is needed for the same effect. Potency and efficacy are different things. A drug can be very potent but have a low maximum effect, and a less potent drug can still be more useful if it reaches a higher maximum or if its effective dose is well tolerated. Drug discovery teams compare IC50 values to rank compounds, often expressed as pIC50, the negative logarithm, so that bigger numbers mean more potent compounds. An IC50 depends on the assay conditions, such as how much natural substrate is present, so values from different laboratories are not always directly comparable.

question.prompt: Compound X has an IC50 of 10 nanomolar and compound Y an IC50 of 1 micromolar against the same target. Which is more potent?

options.text: Compound Y, because its number is larger
They are equally potent
Potency cannot be judged from IC50
Compound X, because less of it is needed to halve the target's activity

question.explanation: A lower IC50 means less compound is needed for the same inhibition; 10 nM is 100 times lower than 1 µM.

items.title: Bioavailability and first-pass metabolism
items.explainer: Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose that reaches the general circulation unchanged. A drug injected into a vein has a bioavailability of 100 percent by definition. A drug swallowed as a tablet usually has less, because it faces several obstacles on the way. It must dissolve in the gut fluids, cross the intestinal wall, and then survive first-pass metabolism. Blood from the intestines does not go straight to the rest of the body; it first passes through the liver via the portal vein, and enzymes in the gut wall and liver can break down a large share of the drug before it ever reaches the heart. Morphine taken by mouth, for example, has a bioavailability of roughly 20 to 40 percent, so oral doses are higher than injected ones. Some drugs are broken down almost completely: glyceryl trinitrate, used for angina, is given under the tongue or through the skin, routes that bypass the liver. Bioavailability is affected by food, other drugs, and differences in people's enzymes. It also matters for generic medicines, which must show bioequivalence to the original, meaning that the amount and rate of drug reaching the blood fall within set limits, before they can be approved. Medicinal chemists tune molecules to improve solubility, permeability and metabolic stability.

question.prompt: Why is glyceryl trinitrate for angina given under the tongue rather than swallowed?

options.text: The sublingual route bypasses the liver, avoiding extensive first-pass metabolism
It tastes bitter
Swallowed tablets dissolve too slowly to ever work
It can only be absorbed through bone

question.explanation: Absorption under the tongue enters the general circulation directly, avoiding the portal vein and liver that would destroy most of an oral dose.

items.title: Cytochrome P450 enzymes and drug interactions
items.explainer: The cytochrome P450 enzymes, often shortened to CYPs, are a family of proteins, mostly in the liver, that break down a large share of medicines. A handful of them, especially CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, together handle the majority of drugs in common use. They typically add an oxygen atom to a drug molecule, making it more water-soluble so that it can be excreted, and often less active. Because so many drugs share the same few enzymes, they are a major source of drug interactions. An inhibitor of an enzyme slows the breakdown of other drugs that rely on it, so their levels rise and side effects can appear. Grapefruit juice is a famous example: compounds in it inhibit CYP3A4 in the gut wall, which can multiply the blood levels of some statins and blood pressure drugs. An inducer does the opposite, making the liver produce more enzyme, so other drugs are cleared faster and may stop working; the antibiotic rifampicin and the herbal remedy St John's wort can make hormonal contraceptives fail this way. People also differ genetically. Some carry CYP2D6 variants that make them poor metabolizers and others carry extra copies that make them ultrarapid metabolizers, which matters for drugs such as codeine, which CYP2D6 converts into morphine.

question.prompt: A patient starts taking a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor alongside a drug cleared by CYP3A4. What is the likely result?

options.text: Levels of the second drug fall and it may stop working
Levels of the second drug rise, increasing the risk of side effects
Nothing changes, because the drugs are different
The inhibitor is excreted faster

question.explanation: Inhibiting the enzyme slows clearance of drugs that depend on it, so their blood levels rise.

items.title: Prodrugs
items.explainer: A prodrug is a medicine given in an inactive or less active form that the body converts into the active drug. Chemists design prodrugs to get around problems with the active molecule itself, such as poor absorption from the gut, a bad taste, instability, or side effects at the wrong site. The conversion is usually carried out by enzymes, often in the liver, the blood or the target tissue. Some well-known medicines are prodrugs. Codeine is converted into morphine by the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which is why it works poorly in people with low activity of that enzyme. Enalapril, a blood pressure drug, is converted into its active form, enalaprilat, which is poorly absorbed when taken by mouth itself. Valaciclovir is a prodrug of the antiviral aciclovir that is absorbed much better, so it can be taken less often. The blood thinner clopidogrel must be activated by liver enzymes too. Levodopa, used for Parkinson's disease, is a different kind of example: dopamine itself cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, but levodopa can, and it is converted into dopamine once it reaches the brain. Prodrugs can also target tissues: some cancer prodrugs are designed to be activated only by enzymes or conditions found in tumors, sparing healthy cells.

question.prompt: Why is levodopa given for Parkinson's disease instead of dopamine itself?

options.text: Dopamine is too expensive
Levodopa is a stronger receptor agonist than dopamine
Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, but levodopa can and is converted to dopamine in the brain
Dopamine is destroyed by stomach acid only

question.explanation: Levodopa crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine there, which dopamine given directly could not do.

items.title: Molecular docking and virtual screening
items.explainer: Virtual screening uses computers to search large libraries of molecules for ones likely to bind a drug target, so that only the most promising need to be made and tested in the laboratory. The most common structure-based approach is molecular docking. Starting from a three-dimensional structure of the target protein, from X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy or a prediction such as AlphaFold, the software tries many positions, orientations and shapes of each candidate molecule in the binding pocket. A scoring function then estimates how well each pose fits, rewarding favorable contacts such as hydrogen bonds and penalizing clashes. Modern libraries are enormous: make-on-demand collections of compounds that suppliers can synthesize within weeks now run to billions of molecules, and docking campaigns have screened hundreds of millions of them against a single target. Docking is fast but approximate. Scoring functions are crude estimates of binding energy, proteins flex in ways a rigid model misses, and water molecules in the pocket are hard to account for, so most top-ranked compounds turn out not to bind. Hit rates of a few percent to tens of percent are nevertheless far better than random testing. Ligand-based methods, which search for molecules resembling known active compounds, are a common alternative when no structure is available.

question.prompt: What is a key limitation of docking scoring functions?

options.text: They require a living animal
They can only score one molecule per year
They work without any target structure
They are approximate estimates of binding, so many top-ranked compounds do not actually bind

question.explanation: Scoring functions simplify binding physics, flexibility and water, so docking enriches for binders but produces many false positives.

items.title: Fragment-based drug discovery
items.explainer: Fragment-based drug discovery starts from very small molecules, typically under about 300 daltons, instead of the larger drug-like compounds used in high-throughput screening. The reasoning is combinatorial. The number of possible small fragments is far smaller than the number of possible drug-sized molecules, so a library of a few thousand fragments covers chemical space much more thoroughly than a library of a million larger compounds. Because fragments are small, they bind only weakly, often with affinities in the high micromolar to millimolar range, too weak for ordinary assays to detect. Sensitive biophysical methods are used instead, such as X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy and surface plasmon resonance. A crystal structure showing exactly where a fragment sits in the binding pocket is especially valuable, because chemists can then grow the fragment by adding groups that reach nearby pockets, or link two fragments that bind side by side. A useful measure is ligand efficiency, the binding energy per heavy atom, which shows whether a fragment makes good contacts for its size. Starting efficient and growing carefully tends to give leads with better properties than starting large. Vemurafenib, approved in 2011 for melanoma with a BRAF mutation, was the first approved drug developed this way, and several others, including venetoclax, have followed.

question.prompt: Why do fragment screens rely on biophysical methods such as X-ray crystallography and NMR?

options.text: Fragments bind so weakly that ordinary activity assays usually cannot detect them
Fragments are too large for ordinary assays
Biophysical methods are cheaper than all other assays
Fragments are always toxic to cells

question.explanation: Fragment affinities are often micromolar to millimolar, so sensitive structural or biophysical techniques are needed to see binding.

items.title: Targeted protein degradation and PROTACs
items.explainer: Most drugs work by blocking a protein's activity, which requires a pocket where a small molecule can bind and switch the protein off. Many disease proteins, such as scaffolding proteins and some transcription factors, have no such pocket and have been considered undruggable. Targeted protein degradation takes a different approach: instead of inhibiting the protein, it gets the cell to destroy it. Cells already have a disposal system, in which enzymes called E3 ubiquitin ligases tag unwanted proteins with chains of the small protein ubiquitin, marking them for destruction by the proteasome. A PROTAC, short for proteolysis-targeting chimera, is a molecule with two ends joined by a linker. One end binds the target protein and the other binds an E3 ligase, such as cereblon or VHL, bringing the two together so the ligase tags the target for degradation. The idea was first described by Craig Crews and Raymond Deshaies in 2001. Because a PROTAC is released after each target is tagged, one molecule can trigger the destruction of many protein copies, and weak binding can be enough. Molecular glues are smaller molecules that achieve the same pairing without a linker; thalidomide and lenalidomide turned out to work this way, by reshaping cereblon. PROTACs are large molecules, so making them orally absorbed is a major challenge.

question.prompt: How does a PROTAC eliminate its target protein?

options.text: By blocking the target's active site permanently
By bringing the target together with an E3 ubiquitin ligase so it is tagged and destroyed by the proteasome
By cutting the target's gene out of the DNA
By preventing the target's messenger RNA from being made

question.explanation: The two-headed molecule recruits an E3 ligase to the target, which ubiquitinates it and sends it to the proteasome.

items.title: Antibody-drug conjugates
items.explainer: Chemotherapy drugs kill dividing cells, but they cannot tell cancer cells from healthy ones, which causes severe side effects and limits how much can be given. An antibody-drug conjugate, or ADC, combines the precision of an antibody with the killing power of a toxic drug. It has three parts. The antibody recognizes a protein that is abundant on the surface of cancer cells, such as HER2 in some breast cancers. A highly potent cytotoxic drug, the payload, is often far too toxic to give on its own. A chemical linker joins them and is designed to stay stable in the blood but release the payload once the ADC has been taken inside the cancer cell. After the antibody binds its target, the cell engulfs the whole complex, and enzymes or acidic conditions inside it cut the linker, freeing the payload to kill the cell. Some payloads can also leak out and kill neighboring cancer cells that lack the target, a bystander effect. The number of drug molecules on each antibody, the drug-to-antibody ratio, affects both potency and side effects. Early ADCs were held back by unstable linkers and modest payloads. Newer ones, such as trastuzumab deruxtecan, have shown striking results, and more than a dozen ADCs have now been approved for cancer.

question.prompt: What is the role of the linker in an antibody-drug conjugate?

options.text: It makes the antibody recognize the tumor
It neutralizes the payload permanently
It keeps the payload attached in the bloodstream and releases it inside the target cell
It replaces the antibody's binding site

question.explanation: A good linker is stable in circulation but is cleaved inside the cancer cell, so the toxic payload acts mainly where it is needed.

items.title: Biomarkers and surrogate endpoints
items.explainer: A biomarker is a measurable sign of a biological state, such as blood pressure, cholesterol level, a gene mutation in a tumor, or the amount of a protein in the blood. In drug development, biomarkers help choose the right patients, confirm that a drug is hitting its target and give early hints of whether it works. A surrogate endpoint is a biomarker used in place of the outcome that patients actually care about, such as survival, heart attacks or quality of life. Surrogates are attractive because they change sooner and need smaller trials. Lowering blood pressure, for instance, reliably reduces strokes, so blood pressure is an accepted surrogate, and regulators such as the FDA can grant accelerated approval on the basis of a surrogate that is reasonably likely to predict benefit, with confirmatory trials required afterwards. The risk is that a drug can improve the surrogate without improving the real outcome, or even while making it worse. In the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, reported in 1989, drugs that suppressed irregular heartbeats after a heart attack, a seemingly sensible surrogate, actually increased deaths. Torcetrapib raised HDL, the so-called good cholesterol, but also increased deaths and cardiovascular events. A surrogate is trustworthy only when trials have shown that changing it changes the real outcome.

question.prompt: What did the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial illustrate about surrogate endpoints?

options.text: Surrogates always predict real outcomes
Blood pressure is not a valid surrogate
Surrogates make trials larger and slower
A drug can improve a surrogate while worsening the outcome that matters, here increasing deaths

question.explanation: The drugs suppressed arrhythmias, the surrogate, yet increased mortality, the real outcome.
